opus-5.5.text:
I think the key point is that architectures don't win in a vacuum. They win because they fit the hardware of their time. Before the Transformer, RNNs and LSTMs were the dominant sequence models, and on paper they're quite elegant: constant memory per step, linear cost in sequence length. But they're fundamentally sequential. You have to finish step t before you can compute step t+1. That's a terrible match for GPUs, which are massively parallel machines that want to do huge matrix multiplications all at once.

The Transformer threw away that recurrence. With self-attention, every token can attend to every other token, and during training you can process the whole sequence in parallel as a few big matmuls. Yes, attention is quadratic in sequence length, so in a theoretical sense it's more expensive. But in practice, FLOPs on GPUs, especially on tensor cores, became so cheap that the quadratic cost mattered less than being able to saturate the hardware. Something that's theoretically more expensive but runs at high utilization can beat something theoretically cheaper that leaves the chip idle.

So when I say the Transformer was "chosen" by its hardware, I mean there's a kind of co-evolution. NVIDIA kept optimizing for dense matrix multiplication, and the Transformer is basically a stack of dense matrix multiplications plus a softmax. Then work like FlashAttention made it even more hardware-friendly by being IO-aware, minimizing reads and writes to slow HBM and keeping things in fast on-chip SRAM. The architecture and the hardware reinforced each other. Sara Hooker calls this the "hardware lottery": ideas succeed partly because they happen to suit the available hardware, not only because they're intrinsically better.

That's also why I think about my own work on linear attention and efficient sequence models this way. It's not enough to propose something with nicer asymptotic complexity. Many earlier linear attention or state-space variants looked great on paper but ran slower than optimized softmax attention in wall-clock time, because they weren't designed around how GPUs actually work. With things like chunkwise parallel forms, you can turn the recurrence into chunks that are processed with matmuls, so you keep the efficiency of recurrence at inference time but still train in a hardware-efficient, parallel way. Things like gated DeltaNet came out of that line of thinking.

And looking forward, the constraints are shifting. Training is no longer the only thing that matters. Inference, long context, and reasoning with very long generations all make the KV cache and memory bandwidth a real bottleneck. When the dominant workload changes, and the hardware changes with it, the best architecture may change too. That's why I think we're already seeing hybrid models that mix attention with linear or recurrent layers. The Transformer was the right answer for its generation of hardware and workloads, and the next generation may choose something a bit different.

r001.rationale: It contrasts sequential RNN/LSTM steps with self-attention processing the whole sequence in parallel as large matrix multiplications, which better suits GPUs.

r002.rationale: It says attention is theoretically more expensive yet can run faster through high hardware utilization, and notes that better asymptotic complexity alone does not ensure faster wall-clock time.

r003.rationale: It says each token can attend to every other token, but does not identify solving long-range dependency problems as a reason for the Transformer's popularity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that architectures don't win because they're the most elegant mathematically. They win because they map well onto the hardware that exists at the moment they appear, and the Transformer appeared at almost exactly the right time for GPUs.

If you look at what a GPU is good at, it's dense matrix multiplication. Tensor cores are basically machines for doing large matmuls very fast, and everything else, memory movement, elementwise operations, sequential dependencies, is comparatively slow. The Transformer is almost entirely matmuls. Attention is QK transpose, then softmax, then multiply by V. The MLP is two big matmuls. There's almost nothing in it that resists parallelization across the sequence dimension during training. You can throw an entire sequence at the hardware in one shot and keep the tensor cores saturated.

Compare that to RNNs, which were the dominant sequence model right before. An LSTM has a recurrence: step t depends on step t minus 1. That's a sequential dependency, and it means during training you're fundamentally limited by sequence length in how much you can parallelize. You can batch across sequences, but you can't batch across time. On a GPU that's a terrible fit. You end up with lots of small kernel launches, poor utilization, memory bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. So even though RNNs are in some sense a more natural model of sequential data, with constant memory per step and no quadratic cost, they lost, and I'd argue they lost mostly for hardware reasons rather than modeling reasons.

Then there's a second layer, which is that once an architecture gets a head start, the hardware and software ecosystem co-evolve around it. FlashAttention is a good example. The quadratic attention cost looked like a fundamental weakness, and then people realized you could restructure the computation to be IO-aware, keep everything in SRAM, fuse the softmax, and suddenly attention is close to the roofline of the hardware. NVIDIA started adding features that make Transformers specifically faster, FP8, the transformer engine on Hopper. So the hardware is now partly designed for the Transformer, which makes the Transformer look even more inevitable in hindsight. It's a feedback loop.

The reason I frame it as "chosen by its generation of hardware" rather than just "the best architecture" is that this framing tells you what to look at going forward. The question for linear attention or state space models or any alternative isn't just whether the math is nicer. It's whether you can express the computation in a form that the current accelerators like, which mostly means can you turn the recurrence back into matmuls. That's really what the chunkwise parallel formulation is about. You trade a little bit of the pure recurrent structure to get a form where most of the FLOPs land on tensor cores, and then suddenly a linear RNN can train as fast or faster than attention at long context. Hardware picked the Transformer in 2017. If the hardware changes, or if we get better at speaking the hardware's language with a different model class, the choice isn't permanent.

r001.rationale: It explains that Transformer attention consists largely of matrix multiplications that suit GPUs, while LSTM recurrence limits parallelism across time.

r002.rationale: It notes that RNNs have constant memory per step and no quadratic cost, yet lost to Transformers largely for hardware reasons, showing that theoretical cost advantages do not guarantee faster execution.

r003.rationale: It does not identify attention’s ability to solve long-range dependency problems as a reason for Transformer popularity.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an architecture succeeds partly because of how well it matches the hardware available to train it. With Transformers, a lot of the work can be expressed as large matrix multiplications, which are exactly the operations GPUs are designed to execute efficiently.

Compare that with a recurrent model. During training, you generally have to process the sequence step by step, because each hidden state depends on the previous one. A Transformer lets you process many positions in parallel. That makes it much easier to use the compute capacity of a GPU and to scale training across many GPUs.

So when I say it was chosen by its generation of hardware, I mean that its success comes from the interaction between the model and the machine. It’s not just an abstract question of which architecture is more expressive. It’s also: with a fixed amount of time and compute, which architecture can you train most effectively?

And that relationship can change. If the balance between computation, memory capacity, and data movement changes, a different architecture might become more attractive. The hardware helps determine which ideas are practical enough to scale.

r002.rationale: It discusses efficient execution on GPUs, but does not state that lower theoretical computational complexity may fail to produce faster hardware execution.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention attention solving long-range dependency problems as a reason for Transformer popularity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an architecture succeeds partly because it fits the hardware available to train it. Transformers are a particularly good fit for GPUs: most of their computation can be expressed as large matrix multiplications, which GPUs execute very efficiently.

If you compare that with a recurrent model, the recurrence creates a dependency across time. You have to process one step before you can process the next. A Transformer lets you process all the tokens in a training sequence in parallel. That makes it much easier to use a large amount of compute effectively.

Of course, attention has a cost: as the sequence gets longer, the number of pairwise interactions grows quadratically. But for the workloads where Transformers took off, the benefit of parallel computation was very powerful.

So when I say the hardware chose the architecture, I mean that model quality alone doesn’t determine what wins. It’s also how efficiently you can train the model, how well it scales, and how well its operations map onto the machine. Different hardware—or even a different balance between training and inference—can favor different architectural choices.

r001.rationale: The response says Transformers’ computation is largely large matrix multiplications that GPUs execute efficiently, contrasting this with sequential recurrence in RNNs.

r002.rationale: It mentions attention’s quadratic cost and hardware efficiency, but does not state that lower theoretical computational complexity may fail to yield faster hardware execution.

r003.rationale: It does not identify attention’s ability to address long-range dependency problems as a reason for Transformer popularity.
